Sheet

Thermodynamics cheat sheet

43 min read

Built from the slides (thermo.tex, thermo-l3.tex, thermo-l4.tex), the tutorial, Atkins 11e and the four teaching docs. Material tagged [A] is in Atkins but not in the slides, and [S] is in the slides only. Everything else is in both. Homework items are tagged like (E2A.4).

0. Before anything else

Sign conventions (the most common way to lose marks)

ΔU=q+wq, w=energy INTO the system
Quantity Positive when Negative when
q (heat) heat flows in heat flows out
w (work) work is done ON the system (compression) the system does work (expansion)
  • Slides and Atkins: w=−∫pex​dV.
  • The tutorial slides use the opposite convention (W = work done BY the gas, ΔU=Q−W). If a question says "work done by", flip the sign and state it.
  • Engines (L3): QH​, QC​, W are magnitudes, with W=QH​−QC​.
  • The Clausius inequality uses signed heats.

Constants and handy numbers (no calculator)

Quantity Value
R 8.314 J K−1mol−1=0.08314 L bar K−1mol−1=0.08206 L atm K−1mol−1
kB​=R/NA​ 1.381×10−23 J K−1
NA​ 6.022×1023 mol−1
F 96485 C mol−1
1 bar, 1 atm 105 Pa, 1.01325×105 Pa
1 L bar 100 J
RT 2.48 kJ/mol at 298 K; 2.49 kJ/mol at 300 K; RT = 24.8 L bar/mol at 298 K
Vm​ (perfect gas) 24.79 L/mol at SATP (298 K, 1 bar); 22.41 L/mol at 273 K, 1 atm
logarithms ln2=0.693, ln3=1.099, ln10=2.303, ln(1+x)≈x for small x
powers 100.4=2.51, 101.4=25.1, 82/3=4, 85/3=32, 8−0.4=0.435
square roots 2​=1.414, 3​=1.732, 8/π​=1.596

Unit traps

  • M in kg/mol for speeds (N₂: 0.028).
  • T in kelvin everywhere.
  • Match R to your units: with L bar, the answer comes out in L bar, and ×100 gives J.
  • Δ always means final minus initial. Always write the sign.

Answering style (90 min, short answers, verbosity is penalised)

State the principle, then the equation, then substitute with units, then box the answer, then one line on sign or meaning. Marking schemes reward each of these steps.

1A The perfect gas (Atkins p.4–10; slides thermo.tex 62–272)

System vocabulary

Term Meaning
Open / closed / isolated exchanges matter and energy / energy only / neither
Diathermic / adiabatic wall lets heat through / does not
Intensive / extensive independent of amount (p, T, ρ, Vm​) / proportional to amount (V, n, U, H, S)
State / path function depends only on state (U, H, S, p, V, T) / depends on route (q, w)
Equilibrium properties uniform and unchanging; thermal (same T), mechanical (same p), chemical

Zeroth law

If A ~ C and B ~ C are in thermal equilibrium, then A ~ B. This makes temperature well defined, and C is a thermometer.

  • Cold bench: metal and wood are at the same T. Metal feels colder because it conducts heat from the skin faster, and touch senses heat flow, not temperature.

Gas thermometer and the Kelvin scale

At constant V, p∝T:

T=T3​p3​p​,T3​=273.16 K (triple point of water)
  • All gases, in the limit p→0, extrapolate to p=0 at θ=−273.15 ∘C.
  • T/K=θ/∘C+273.15.
  • Tutorial P1: 6.69 kPa at T3​ gives 9.14 kPa at 100 °C. A reading of 8.00 kPa means 326.6 K = 53.5 °C.
  • (P1A.2) For a new scale based on two fixed points, plot p against θ, which is linear. Absolute zero is where the line meets p=0. Convert it to the new scale by linear interpolation.

Gas laws and the perfect gas equation

Law Statement Held constant
Boyle pV = const n, T
Charles V∝T (and p∝T) n, p (or V)
Avogadro V∝n p, T
pV=nRT=NkB​TT1​p1​V1​​=T2​p2​V2​​ (fixed n)
  • It is a limiting law: exact only as p→0.
  • (Ex 1A.1) Heating at constant V: p2​=p1​T2​/T1​. 100 atm at 300 K becomes 167 atm at 500 K.

Molar mass from density (E1A.9)

ρ=Vm​=RTpM​⇒M=pρRT​

Mixtures [A] (Ex 1A.2, E1A.11)

xJ​=nnJ​​,J∑​xJ​=1,pJ​=xJ​p,p=J∑​pJ​ (Dalton)
  • For a perfect gas, each component behaves as if alone: pJ​=nJ​RT/V.
  • From a mass composition, divide each mass by its M to get moles, then take mole fractions.

Barometric formula [A] (P1A.11)

dhdp​=−ρg=−RTpMg​⇒p=p0​e−h/H,H=MgRT​≈8 km

1B The kinetic model (Atkins p.11–18; slides thermo.tex 277–440, 504–539)

Assumptions

  1. Molecules of mass m are in ceaseless random motion.
  2. Their size is negligible compared with the distances travelled.
  3. They do not interact except in brief elastic collisions.

Pressure derivation (memorise the skeleton)

  1. One molecule hits the wall: Δpx​=2mvx​. The time between hits on the same wall is 2L/vx​, so F=mvx2​/L.
  2. Sum over N molecules and divide by L2: p=Nm⟨vx2​⟩/V.
  3. Isotropy gives ⟨vx2​⟩=⟨vy2​⟩=⟨vz2​⟩=31​⟨v2⟩.
pV=31​Nm⟨v2⟩=32​N⟨Ek​⟩
  1. Compare with pV=NkB​T:
⟨Ek​⟩=21​m⟨v2⟩=23​kB​T​(per mole: 23​RT)

T measures the average translational KE. It is independent of mass.

Characteristic speeds (all ∝T/M​)

Speed Formula N₂, 300 K
most probable vmp​=2RT/M​ 422 m/s
mean vmean​=8RT/πM​ 476 m/s
root mean square vrms​=3RT/M​ 517 m/s
mean relative [A] vrel​=2​vmean​ (same species) 674 m/s
  • The ratio vmp​:vmean​:vrms​=1:1.128:1.225. They are ordered this way because of the long high-speed tail.
  • Other vrms​ values: He at 300 K is 1.37 km/s. At 20 °C (E1B.2), H₂ is 1.90 km/s and O₂ is 0.48 km/s.
  • Doubling T multiplies speeds by 2​, not 2. At the same T, v∝1/M​, so H₂ is 4× faster than O₂.

Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution

f(v)=4π(2πRTM​)3/2v2e−Mv2/2RT
  • The v2 factor: more ways (a bigger spherical shell) to have higher speed.
  • The exponential: high energies are rare.
  • Higher T or lower M: the peak moves right, and the curve gets broader and flatter. The area is always 1.
  • vmp​ (P1B.10, tutorial P3a): set dvd​(v2e−Mv2/2RT)=(2v−RTMv3​)e⋯=0. This gives v2=2RT/M.
  • Fraction in a narrow window: ΔN/N≈f(v)Δv (tutorial P3b: about 0.9 %).
  • Mean speed (Ex 1B.1): vmean​=∫0∞​vf(v)dv=8RT/πM​.
  • Escape (P1B.7, tutorial P2): vesc​=2gRplanet​​, which is 11.2 km/s for Earth. Setting v=vesc​ gives the temperature at which that happens. Light gases escape even at low T, because a fraction of molecules in the high-speed tail always exceeds vesc​ and collisions keep refilling the tail.

Collisions [A] (E1B.8)

Quantity Formula
collision cross-section σ=πd2 (d = molecular diameter); N₂ ≈ 0.40 nm², Ar 0.36 nm²
collision frequency z=σvrel​VN​=kB​Tσvrel​p​ (N₂ at 1 atm, 300 K: 6.6×109 s−1)
mean free path λ=zvrel​​=σpkB​T​ (about 100 nm at 1 atm)
  • λ∝1/p at fixed T. To make λ equal a length L, set p=kB​T/(σL).

Concept checks

  • H₂ and O₂ at the same T have the same ⟨Ek​⟩. H₂ has 4× the vrms​.
  • Doubling T at constant V raises vrms​ by a factor of 2​ and doubles p.
  • The total translational KE of a gas is 23​pV, independent of the species (tutorial P2b).

1C Real gases (Atkins p.19–27; slides thermo.tex 445–499)

Compression factor

Z=RTpVm​​Z=1 perfect;Z<1 attractions dominate;Z>1 repulsions dominate (high p)

The perfect gas law fails at high p (molecular size matters) and low T (attractions matter).

Virial equation [A]

pVm​=RT(1+Vm​B​+Vm2​C​+⋯)
  • B(T) is the second virial coefficient. At the Boyle temperature, B=0 and the gas behaves nearly perfectly over a range of p.
  • For a van der Waals gas, B=b−a/RT, so TB​=a/(Rb).

van der Waals equation

(p+Vm2​a​)(Vm​−b)=RT⟺p=Vm​−bRT​−Vm2​a​
Term Meaning
b excluded volume per mole (repulsion), which raises p
a/Vm2​ pressure reduction from attractions; it scales as (n/V)2 because attraction needs pairs
Gas a / L² bar mol⁻² b / L mol⁻¹
He 0.0346 0.0238
N₂ 1.370 0.0387
CO₂ 3.640 0.0427
  • Tutorial P4 (5 mol in 1 L at 298 K): pideal​ = 124 bar. N₂ gives 119 bar (Z = 0.96, a wins). He gives 140 bar (Z = 1.13, b wins).
  • Slide example: 1 mol CO₂ in 0.5 L at 300 K gives pideal​ = 49.9 bar but pvdW​ = 54.5 − 14.6 = 40.0 bar.

Critical point and corresponding states [A]

  • At the critical point the isotherm has a horizontal inflection: (∂p/∂Vm​)T​=0 and (∂2p/∂Vm2​)T​=0. These give:
Vc​=3b,Tc​=27Rb8a​,pc​=27b2a​,Zc​=RTc​pc​Vc​​=83​
  • Below Tc​, vdW isotherms show unphysical loops. They are replaced by a flat line drawn so that the areas above and below are equal (the Maxwell construction): that line is liquid–vapour coexistence.
  • Reduced variables are pr​=p/pc​, Tr​=T/Tc​, Vr​=Vm​/Vc​. Corresponding states: real gases at the same Tr​ and Vr​ have about the same pr​ and the same Z.
  • Reduced vdW equation: pr​=3Vr​−18Tr​​−Vr2​3​. It contains no a or b.
  • Characteristic temperatures for a vdW gas: Tc​=278​TB​, TB​=a/Rb, TI​=2a/Rb=2TB​. For N₂ these are 126, 426 and 852 K.

2A Internal energy (Atkins p.34–45; slides thermo.tex 600–867, 1124–1352)

Work and heat

  • Work: energy transfer that uses organised motion in the surroundings (a weight falls, a piston moves). It could in principle raise a weight.
  • Heat: energy transfer driven by a temperature difference, using disorderly thermal motion.
  • Both describe energy in transit. A body contains neither.
  • Joule's paddle wheel: 4.18 J of work has the same effect as 1 cal of heat.
  • Exothermic means it releases heat (q<0). Endothermic means it absorbs heat.

First law

U is a state function. For a closed system, ΔU=q+w; for an isolated system, ΔU=0.

dU=dq+dw,∮dU=0,∮dq=0

Expansion work

dw=−pex​dV
Process Work on the gas
free expansion (pex​=0) w=0
constant pex​ w=−pex​ΔV
reversible (pex​=p at every step) w=−∫pdV
reversible isothermal, perfect gas w=−nRTlnVi​Vf​​=−nRTlnpf​pi​​
gas produced at constant pex​ (Ex 2A.1) w=−pex​ΔV=−ngas​RT; a closed fixed vessel gives w=0
  • ∣w∣ is the area under the path on a p–V diagram, so work depends on the path.
  • Reversible means maximum work out. At every step pex​ is as large as it can be without stopping the expansion. Any irreversible route gives less.
  • Slide example: 1 mol, 300 K, 10 → 20 L reversibly gives w=−RTln2=−1.73 kJ, and q=+1.73 kJ.
  • Slide two-route example (A: 1 bar, 20 L to C: 2 bar, 10 L): route 1 gives w=+1.0 kJ, route 2 gives w=+2.0 kJ. ΔU=0 on both because TA​=TC​, so q=−1.0 and −2.0 kJ.

Model results: E2A.4 type (1 mol perfect gas, 293 K, 10 → 30 L)

Route w q ΔU
reversible isothermal −RTln3=−2.68 kJ +2.68 kJ 0
against constant pex​=pf​ −pf​ΔV=−RT(20/30)=−1.62 kJ +1.62 kJ 0
free (vacuum) 0 0 0

ΔU=0 in every case because T is constant and the gas is perfect. Only the split between q and w changes.

Work with an equation of state (P2A.6)

For p=nRT/V−n2a/V2:

w=−nRTlnVi​Vf​​+n2a(Vi​1​−Vf​1​)

The second term is positive on expansion, so less work is done on the surroundings than by a perfect gas. Attractions hold the gas back.

Other kinds of work [S] (Atkins Table 2A.1; Zemansky ch.3)

General form: dw=YdX, with Y an intensive "force" and X an extensive "displacement".

System dw (on the system)
gas −pdV
wire / rubber band +FdL (plus sign: tension pulls inward). For Hooke's law F=k(L−L0​): w=21​k(L−L0​)2
surface film γdA. A soap film has two faces: dA=2ℓdx
electrochemical cell EdZ (Atkins: ϕdQ). Reversible: W=nFE
dielectric slab EdΠ
paramagnet μ0​HdM. Curie's law: M=CC​H/T
  • Generalised first law: dU=dq−pdV+FdL+γdA+EdZ+⋯
  • Atkins: dU=dq+dwexp​+dwadd​.
  • (P2A.3) Elastomer: w=∫0x​Fdx with the given F(x). For kf​(x)=a−bx1/2, F=(a−bx1/2)x and w=21​ax2−52​bx5/2.

Molecular interpretation and equipartition

  • Each quadratic term in the energy contributes 21​kB​T per molecule.
Molecule Translational Rotational Um​−Um​(0) CV,m​
monatomic 3 0 23​RT 23​R
linear 3 2 25​RT 25​R
nonlinear 3 3 3RT 3R
  • Vibrations are frozen at room T, which is why N₂ is not 27​R. An active vibrational mode adds kB​T (kinetic + potential).
  • For a perfect gas, U depends only on T.

Heat capacity and calorimetry

CV​=(∂T∂U​)V​,ΔU=qV​=CV​ΔT  (constant V, CV​ constant)
  • Bomb calorimeter [A] works at constant V, so it measures ΔU. Calibrate first: Ccal​=q/ΔT, using a known reaction or electrical heating q=IVt. Then q=Ccal​ΔT.
  • (E2C.4) Calorimeter constant from a standard: Ccal​=n∣Δc​U∣/ΔT. For the second sample, ΔT=n′∣Δc​U′∣/Ccal​. Get Δc​U from Δc​H using Δng​RT (see 2B).

2B Enthalpy (Atkins p.46–50; slides thermo.tex 893–937, 989–1022)

Definition

H=U+pV,dH=dq  (constant p, no extra work) ⇒ ΔH=qp​
  • H is a state function.
  • Reactions with gases [A]: ΔH=ΔU+Δng​RT, where Δng​ = moles of gas in products minus reactants (E2B.2, E2C.6).
    • Example: N2​+3H2​→2NH3​ has Δng​=−2, so ΔHm​−ΔUm​=−2RT=−4.96 kJ/mol at 298 K.
    • Condensed phases: ΔH≈ΔU.

Heat capacity at constant pressure

Cp​=(∂T∂H​)p​,ΔH=∫T1​T2​​Cp​dT
  • Temperature-dependent [A]: Cp,m​=a+bT+c/T2 (Table 2B.1). Then (Ex 2B.2, E2B.3)
ΔHm​=a(T2​−T1​)+21​b(T22​−T12​)−c(T2​1​−T1​1​)
  • E2B.3 recipe for Cp​=α+βT:
    • At constant p: q=ΔH, w=−nRΔT, ΔU=ΔH−nRΔT.
    • At constant V: w=0, and ΔU and ΔH are the same as at constant p (both state functions, perfect gas, same ΔT). So q=ΔU.

Relation between heat capacities (perfect gas)

H=U+nRT⇒Cp​−CV​=nR,Cp,m​−CV,m​=R,γ=CV​Cp​​
Gas CV,m​ Cp,m​ γ
monatomic 23​R 25​R 35​=1.67
diatomic (room T) 25​R 27​R 57​=1.40
  • Physically, Cp​>CV​ because at constant p part of the heat leaves again as expansion work.
  • Slide bookkeeping (1 mol monatomic gas, +100 K at constant p): q=+2.08 kJ, w=−0.83 kJ, ΔU=+1.25 kJ. So 40 % of the heat leaves as work.
  • Concept check: heating the same gas from 300 to 400 K at constant V and at constant p gives the same ΔU, but q is bigger at constant p.
  • (P2B.2) Estimate the moles of air in a room as n=pV/RT, then q=nCp,m​ΔT. Air's small heat capacity is why deserts cool fast at night.

2C Thermochemistry [A] (Atkins p.51–58; not in slides; 7 homework items)

Standard states and physical changes

  • Standard state (°): the pure substance at exactly 1 bar, at the specified T. Tables are at 298.15 K.
  • Phase-change enthalpies: Δsub​H°=Δfus​H°+Δvap​H° (same T). The reverse process has −ΔH.
  • Water: Δfus​H = 6.01 kJ/mol at 273 K; Δvap​H = 40.7 kJ/mol at 373 K.

Hess's law

The standard reaction enthalpy of an overall reaction is the sum of the values for the steps it can be split into (Ex 2C.1). Add and subtract equations, and multiply by coefficients, exactly as you would do with the equations themselves.

Formation enthalpies

  • Δf​H° is the standard enthalpy of forming 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their reference states. For an element in its reference state, Δf​H°=0.
Δr​H°=products∑​νΔf​H°−reactants∑​νΔf​H°(P2C.8)
  • Combustion (Δc​H°) goes to CO₂(g) + H₂O(l), and Δc​H<0.

Kirchhoff's law (temperature dependence)

Δr​H°(T2​)=Δr​H°(T1​)+∫T1​T2​​Δr​Cp​°dT,Δr​Cp​°=prod∑​νCp,m​°−reac∑​νCp,m​°
  • Constant Δr​Cp​°: Δr​H°(T2​)=Δr​H°(T1​)+Δr​Cp​°(T2​−T1​).
  • Ex 2C.2: for H2​+21​O2​→H2​O(g), Δr​Cp​=33.58−28.84−21​(29.37)=−9.95 J/K/mol. So Δf​H°(373 K)=−241.82−0.75=−242.57 kJ/mol.

Calorimetry and DSC

  • A bomb calorimeter gives ΔU. Convert with ΔH=ΔU+Δng​RT (E2C.4, E2C.6).
  • DSC (differential scanning calorimetry) measures the extra heat needed to keep the sample at the reference's temperature during a scan, which gives an excess heat capacity Cp,ex​. Then:
    • Δtrs​H=∫Cp,ex​dT, the area under the peak (P2C.10);
    • the baseline shift across the transition gives ΔCp​.
  • (P2C.1) Body heat: if the body were isolated, ΔT=q/(mc), about 37 K for 10 MJ, 65 kg. The mass of water that must evaporate is q/Δvap​H (per mass), about 4 kg.

2D State functions and exact differentials (Atkins p.59–66; slides thermo.tex 842–862, 1393–1739)

Exact versus inexact

  • df=Mdx+Ndy is exact (so f is a state function) if and only if (∂y∂M​)x​=(∂x∂N​)y​.
  • Then ∫AB​df=fB​−fA​ and ∮df=0.
  • dq and dw are inexact. Hiking analogy: altitude gained is a state function; distance walked is a path function.

Partial-derivative toolkit

Name Relation
reciprocal (∂x/∂y)z​=1/(∂y/∂x)z​
Euler chain (∂x/∂y)z​(∂y/∂z)x​(∂z/∂x)y​=−1
mixed derivatives ∂2f/∂x∂y=∂2f/∂y∂x

Changes in internal energy

dU=CV​dT+πT​dV,πT​=(∂V∂U​)T​=T(∂T∂p​)V​−p

The second formula for πT​ (the thermodynamic equation of state) is derived in 3E: use it, don't derive it.

Gas πT​ Meaning
perfect 0 no interactions, so U=U(T)
van der Waals a/Vm2​>0 only a appears
  • Molecular meaning: at constant T the KE is fixed, so πT​ is the change in potential energy as molecules separate.
    • Attractions dominate: πT​>0, because pulling molecules apart raises their potential energy.
    • Repulsions dominate: πT​<0.
  • Size: N₂ at 1 bar has πT​≈0.002 bar (negligible). Dense CO₂ (0.5 L/mol) has 14.6 bar.
  • Isothermal vdW expansion (E2D.2): ΔUm​=∫πT​dVm​=a(Vm,i​1​−Vm,f​1​). Then w=−∫pdV using the vdW p, and q=ΔU−w.
  • Joule experiment: free expansion has w=0, and Joule saw no ΔT. He concluded πT​=0, but the water bath's huge heat capacity hid the real effect (N₂ doubling cools by about 0.13 K in the gas alone).

Expansion coefficient and compressibility [A]

α=V1​(∂T∂V​)p​,κT​=−V1​(∂p∂V​)T​perfect gas: α=T1​, κT​=p1​  (Ex 2D.2)
(∂T∂U​)p​=απT​V+CV​,Cp​−CV​=κT​α2TV​  (general; =nR for a perfect gas; P2D.2)

I2.5 one-liner. (∂V∂CV​​)T​=∂V∂T∂2U​=(∂T∂πT​​)V​=T(∂T2∂2p​)V​. This is 0 for a perfect gas because p is linear in T.

Changes in enthalpy and the Joule–Thomson effect

dH=Cp​dT+μT​dp,μT​=(∂p∂H​)T​=−Cp​μ  (Euler chain)

Why throttling conserves enthalpy. In steady flow through a porous plug in an insulated tube, q=0. Pushing the gas in and out gives w=pi​Vi​−pf​Vf​. So Uf​−Ui​=pi​Vi​−pf​Vf​, which means Hf​=Hi​: the process is isenthalpic.

μ=(∂p∂T​)H​μ>0: gas cools on expansion;μ<0: gas warms
  • Molecular picture: attractions dominate, so molecules climb out of each other's potential wells and lose kinetic energy, and T falls. Repulsions dominate, so T rises. At high T, repulsions win. For a perfect gas, μ=0.
  • van der Waals, low pressure (P2D.8):
μ≈Cp,m​1​(RT2a​−b),TI​=Rb2a​
  • N₂ at 298 K: μ≈0.25 K/bar (measured 0.27 K/atm). The vdW TI​ is about 850 K; the real value is 621 K.
Gas μ / K atm⁻¹ (298 K) TI​ / K Effect when throttled at room T
CO₂ +1.1 ~1500 cools strongly (extinguisher frosts)
N₂ +0.27 621 cools
H₂ −0.03 ~200 warms
He −0.06 ~40 warms slightly
  • Linde liquefaction:
    1. Compress the gas and remove the heat of compression.
    2. Throttle it, so it cools (only if it is inside the inversion curve).
    3. Use the cold gas to pre-cool the incoming gas in a counter-current heat exchanger.
    4. Repeat until the gas liquefies.
  • H₂ and He must first be pre-cooled below TI​ (H₂ with liquid N₂, He with liquid H₂).
  • Measuring μT​: keep T constant with a heater, and μT​≈−q/Δp per mole.

2E Adiabatic changes (Atkins p.67–69; slides thermo.tex 942–988, 1025–1121)

Reversible adiabatic process, perfect gas (q=0)

dU=dw:nCV,m​dT=−VnRT​dV⇒TdT​=−CV,m​R​VdV​=−(γ−1)VdV​
TVγ−1=const,pVγ=const,Tγp1−γ=const
  • Atkins form: Vi​Tic​=Vf​Tfc​ with c=CV,m​/R. Equivalently Tf​=Ti​(Vi​/Vf​)1/c.
  • Work: wad​=CV​ΔT=γ−1pf​Vf​−pi​Vi​​.
  • Irreversible adiabatic process against a constant pex​: nCV,m​(Tf​−Ti​)=−pex​(Vf​−Vi​). Solve this together with pV=nRT. Do not use pVγ, which holds only for reversible paths.
  • The adiabat is steeper than the isotherm: dVdp​​ad​=−γVp​ against −Vp​. With no heat coming in, the expanding gas cools, so p falls faster.
  • Compression heats the gas; expansion cools it.

Fire syringe (slide example)

Air (γ=1.4) at 1 bar and 300 K is compressed to V/10:

  • T2​=300×100.4=754 K (about 480 °C)
  • p2​=101.4=25 bar

The same physics ignites the fuel in a diesel engine.

The four standard processes (perfect gas)

Process w q ΔU ΔH
isochoric 0 nCV,m​ΔT nCV,m​ΔT nCp,m​ΔT
isobaric −pΔV=−nRΔT nCp,m​ΔT nCV,m​ΔT nCp,m​ΔT
isothermal (rev) −nRTln(Vf​/Vi​) −w 0 0
adiabatic (rev) nCV,m​ΔT 0 nCV,m​ΔT nCp,m​ΔT

ΔU=nCV,m​ΔT in every row, because U depends only on T.

Free expansion versus reversible adiabatic expansion

Both have q=0:

  • Free expansion: w=0, so ΔU=0 and ΔT=0 for a perfect gas.
  • Reversible adiabatic expansion: the gas does work, so it cools.

Same q, different path, different outcome.

3A Entropy: the second law, Carnot, Clausius (Atkins p.78–87; slides all of thermo-l3.tex and thermo-l4.tex 20–99, 188–375)

Cycles and engines

  • Over a cycle ΔU=0, so the net heat in equals the net work out, which is the area enclosed by the loop. A clockwise loop is an engine; an anticlockwise loop is a fridge.
  • Engine (magnitudes): absorbs QH​, does W, rejects QC​.
η=QH​W​=1−QH​QC​​
  • [S] Fridge / heat pump: COPfridge​=WQC​​, COPhp​=WQH​​=1+COPfridge​. COP can exceed 1, because the work moves heat rather than creating it.
    • A heat pump with COP 3.5 delivers 3.5 kJ to the house per 1 kJ of electricity.
  • A fridge left open in a closed kitchen warms the room: the work input ends up as heat in the room.

Second law: two statements

Statement Content
Kelvin–Planck No cyclic device can turn heat from a single reservoir entirely into work, so QC​>0 and η<1 always
Clausius No cyclic device can move heat from cold to hot with no other effect
  • Equivalence proof [S]: suppose a "perfect fridge" moves QC​ from cold to hot with no work. Pair it with an ordinary engine that rejects QC​. The cold reservoir then sees no net change, and the pair turns QH​−QC​ from the hot reservoir entirely into W, which violates Kelvin–Planck. The reverse argument also works.
  • The word "cyclic" matters: an isothermal expansion turns heat entirely into work, but only once.

Reversibility

A process is reversible if it can be run backwards with both the system and the surroundings restored.

  • It needs: a quasi-static process, no dissipation, and heat exchanged only across infinitesimal ΔT.
  • Sources of irreversibility: friction, heat flow across a finite ΔT, free expansion, mixing, resistance, and fast changes.

Carnot cycle (two isotherms and two adiabats)

Step Process Heat Entropy change of gas
1→2 isothermal expansion at TH​ QH​=nRTH​ln(V2​/V1​) in +nRln(V2​/V1​)
2→3 adiabatic expansion, TH​→TC​ 0 0
3→4 isothermal compression at TC​ QC​=nRTC​ln(V3​/V4​) out −nRln(V3​/V4​)
4→1 adiabatic compression, TC​→TH​ 0 0

The adiabats give TH​V2γ−1​=TC​V3γ−1​ and TH​V1γ−1​=TC​V4γ−1​. Dividing one by the other gives V2​/V1​=V3​/V4​, so:

QH​QC​​=TH​TC​​⇒ηCarnot​=1−TH​TC​​​COPfridge,max​=TH​−TC​TC​​,COPhp,max​=TH​−TC​TH​​
  • 500 K / 300 K gives η=0.40. Per 1000 J in: W = 400 J and QC​ = 600 J.
  • P3A.3 numbers (0.10 mol between 373 K and 273 K, V1​=1.00 L doubling, VT3/2 = const on the adiabats):
    • V2​=2.00, V3​=3.19, V4​=1.60 L
    • qH​=+215 J, qC​=−157 J, wnet​=−57.6 J
    • η=0.268, and ΔS=±0.576 J/K on the isotherms

Carnot's theorem

  1. No engine working between two reservoirs beats a reversible engine.
  2. All reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same η, whatever the working substance.

Proof sketch: suppose an engine X beats Carnot. Drive a reversed Carnot engine with X's work. The net effect moves heat from cold to hot with no work input, which violates Clausius.

Thermodynamic temperature: define TC​/TH​≡QC​/QH​ for a reversible engine, fixed by T3​=273.16 K. It is independent of any material, and T=0 would need a 100 % engine.

[S] Otto cycle (two adiabats + two isochores): η=1−r1−γ with r=Vmax​/Vmin​. r=8 gives 0.565; r=10 gives 0.602 (P3B.10).

Checking an inventor's claim (two steps):

  1. First law: does W=QH​−QC​?
  2. Second law: is η≤1−TC​/TH​?

Example: 1000 J in at 400 K, 500 J out at 300 K, W = 500 J. The first law is fine, but η=0.50>0.25, so it is impossible.

From Carnot to entropy

  • With signed heats, Carnot gives QH​/TH​+QC​/TC​=0. Any reversible cycle is a sum of thin Carnot cycles, so
∮Tdqrev​​=0⇒dS=Tdqrev​​ is exact;ΔS=∫if​Tdqrev​​(J K−1)
  • 1/T is an integrating factor: it turns the inexact dqrev​ into the exact dS.
  • To find ΔS for any process, invent a reversible path between the same end states.
  • Surroundings (a large reservoir): ΔSsur​=qsur​/Tsur​=−qsys​/Tsur​, for any process.

Clausius inequality and the principle of entropy increase

∮Tdq​≤0  (=0 only if reversible),dS≥Tdq​,ΔSisolated​≥0,ΔStot​=ΔSsys​+ΔSsur​≥0
  • Heat flow q from TH​ to TC​: ΔStot​=q(TC​1​−TH​1​)>0. For 1000 J from 400 K to 300 K, ΔStot​=+0.83 J/K. The reverse flow would make it negative, which is the Clausius statement.
  • An isolated system reaches equilibrium when S is at its maximum.
  • A system's own S can fall if the surroundings gain more.

Statistical entropy (3A.2(b); slides L4)

S=kB​lnWW=number of microstates consistent with the macrostate
  • Two-box counting: the number of ways to put n of N labelled particles on the left is W=n!(N−n)!N!​.
    • N=4 gives W = 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, with total 24=16.
    • N=6 with 3 left gives W=20.
    • The chance of all N on the left is 2−N; for N=100 that is 8×10−31.
  • The relative width of the distribution is ∼1/N​, so for N∼1023 fluctuations are unmeasurable. "Irreversible" means overwhelmingly improbable to reverse.
  • The logarithm makes S extensive: W=W1​W2​, so S=S1​+S2​.
  • Check against Clausius: when the volume doubles, Wf​/Wi​=2N, so ΔS=NkB​ln2=nRln2, the same as the Clausius result.
  • A perfect crystal at T=0 has W=1 and S=0 (third law, Topic 3C, after this quiz).
  • I3.2 (thermodynamic versus statistical definitions):
    • Clausius: dS=dqrev​/T is measurable, macroscopic, and gives only changes in S.
    • Boltzmann: S=klnW is microscopic, counts arrangements, and gives absolute values.
    • They agree: the gas-expansion check above, and heating, which populates more energy levels so W rises.
    • Heat added at low T produces a larger relative change in the spread of energy than the same heat at high T. That is why 1/T appears in dS=dqrev​/T.

"Entropy = disorder"?

  • Helps: with spreading, mixing and melting, and with seeing why Δvap​S≫Δfus​S.
  • Misleads:
    • a shuffled deck of cards has no thermodynamic ΔS;
    • a supercooled liquid crystallises spontaneously even though the crystal is more ordered, because the released heat raises Ssur​ by more;
    • living things and fridges lower S locally by exporting entropy.
  • Better phrasing: entropy counts the microscopic ways to realise what we observe, or how spread out energy and matter are.

3B Entropy changes in specific processes (Atkins p.88–91; slides thermo-l4.tex 100–187)

Expansion (perfect gas, isothermal)

ΔS=nRlnVi​Vf​​=nRlnpf​pi​​

Gas expanding V→2V (1 mol, 300 K), with ΔS in J/K. It applies to E3A.4(b) as well.

Route ΔSsys​ ΔSsur​ ΔStot​
reversible isothermal +5.76 −5.76 0
free expansion (vacuum) +5.76 0 +5.76
reversible adiabatic 0 (q_rev = 0) 0 0
  • Same end states give the same ΔSsys​; only ΔStot​ tells the routes apart.
  • In a reversible adiabatic expansion T falls, and that loss of entropy exactly cancels the gain from the volume increase.

Phase transitions (at the transition temperature)

Both phases coexist, so heat flows reversibly at constant T:

Δtrs​S=Ttrs​Δtrs​H​
  • Water: fusion gives 6.01 kJ / 273.15 K = 22.0 J/K/mol; vaporisation gives 40.7 kJ / 373.15 K = 109 J/K/mol.
  • Trouton's rule: Δvap​S°≈85 J/K/mol for many liquids, because a similar volume change happens whenever a liquid becomes a gas.
    • Water is higher because hydrogen bonding orders the liquid.
    • Use it to estimate Δvap​H≈85Tb​ J/mol.
  • Vaporisation entropy is much larger than fusion entropy, because a gas has far more accessible arrangements.

Heating

ΔS=∫Ti​Tf​​TCdT​=ClnTi​Tf​​  (C constant);Cp​=a+bT⇒ΔS=alnTi​Tf​​+b(Tf​−Ti​)
  • Use Cp​ at constant p and CV​ at constant V. ΔS is the area under the C/T against T curve.
  • 1.00 kg water, 20 → 80 °C: ΔS=4180ln(353.15/293.15)=+778 J/K.
  • Mixing hot and cold water: 1 kg at 80 °C + 1 kg at 20 °C ends at 50 °C, with
ΔS=mc[lnT1​Tf​​+lnT2​Tf​​]=4180ln353.15×293.15323.152​=+36 J/K>0

Composite processes [A]

Split the change into reversible steps and add the ΔS values.

  • V and T both change (Ex 3B.1):
ΔS=nRlnVi​Vf​​+nCV,m​lnTi​Tf​​(or nCp,m​lnTi​Tf​​−nRlnpi​pf​​)

  • A transition away from Ttrs​ (P3B.2: water ↔ ice at a temperature other than 0 °C). Take three steps:

    1. heat or cool to Ttrs​ (Cp​ln);
    2. transform at Ttrs​ (±ΔH/Ttrs​);
    3. return to the original T (Cp​ln).

    Then ΔSsur​=−ΔHsys​(T)/T, with ΔH(T) from Kirchhoff. If ΔStot​<0, the process is not spontaneous.

  • Freezing in a freezer: ΔSwater​<0, but ΔSuniv​>0, because the heat released and the compressor work raise Ssur​.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Wrong sign of w (check: expansion gives w<0), or mixing up the tutorial and lecture conventions.
  2. M in g/mol inside 3RT/M​.
  3. °C inside ln(Tf​/Ti​), η=1−TC​/TH​ or pV=nRT.
  4. Using pVγ for an irreversible adiabatic process. Only CV​ΔT=−pex​ΔV holds there.
  5. Setting q=0 for an isothermal process. It is ΔU that is 0; q=−w.
  6. Writing ΔU=nCp​ΔT at constant p. It is always nCV​ΔT for a perfect gas; ΔH=nCp​ΔT.
  7. ΔSsys​=0 for free expansion. Wrong: ΔSsys​=nRln(Vf​/Vi​), because you need a reversible path.
  8. ΔS=q/T for an irreversible path. Only qrev​ counts.
  9. v∝T. Wrong: v∝T​, while energy is ∝T.
  10. Treating COP like efficiency, as if it must be < 1. COP can be > 1.
  11. Forgetting the factor 2 for a soap film's two surfaces.
  12. Forgetting Δng​RT when converting bomb-calorimeter ΔU to ΔH.
  13. Using Δf​H=0 for compounds or non-reference forms. It is 0 only for elements in their reference state (e.g. O₂(g), C(graphite)).
  14. Saying "the gas has more heat". Heat is energy in transit; a hotter body has more internal energy.

6. One-line answers to likely "explain" questions

Question Answer
Why does metal feel colder than wood at the same T? It conducts heat from the skin faster; touch senses heat flow, not T.
Why is it called the zeroth law? It was named after the first and second laws, but it is logically prior.
Why does a real gas deviate at high p and low T? Finite size (high p) and attractions (low T) matter.
Why is Cp​>CV​? At constant p, part of the heat does expansion work.
Why is the adiabat steeper? With no heat in, the gas cools as it expands, so p falls faster: γ>1.
Why does He warm when throttled? It is above its inversion temperature (~40 K), so repulsions dominate and μ<0.
Why did Joule miss πT​? The water bath's heat capacity swamped the tiny temperature change.
Why can't a ship run by cooling the ocean? Kelvin–Planck: you need a cold sink; one reservoir can't give net work in a cycle.
Why is reversible work the maximum? pex​ is as high as possible at every step without stopping the expansion.
Why is ηCarnot​ independent of the working substance? Carnot's theorem: otherwise you could violate Clausius.
Why does a fridge with its door open warm the room? The work input ends up as heat in the room.
Why does vaporisation entropy exceed fusion entropy? A gas has vastly more accessible microstates than a liquid.
Why does ln appear in S=klnW? Microstates multiply (W1​W2​) while entropy must add.
How can water freeze spontaneously if ΔSwater​<0? ΔSsur​=+∣ΔH∣/T is larger, so ΔStot​>0.
